newsitem.title: CHINA: North Korea defector crisis moves into seventh day.
newsitem.headline: North Korea defector crisis moves into seventh day.

text.p: A diplomatic crisis centred on the most senior leader ever to flee North Korea moved into its seventh day on Tuesday, despite an apparent softening in Pyongyang's hardline stance on his defection.

Chinese security forces sent three armoured personnel carriers to guard approaches to the South Korean mission in Beijing in a tightening of the cordon around defector Hwang Jang-yop, who sought refuge there last Wednesday.

The boosted protection for Hwang, a top aide to North Korean supreme leader Kim Jong-il, came despite signs that Pyongyang was ready to take a softer line on the three-way diplomatic crisis prompted by his flight.
The official KCNA news agency said late on Monday that North Korea would take strong action if it turned out that Hwang was kidnapped, but that he would be fired if he had sought asylum.
"Our stand is simple and clear. If he was kidnapped, we cannot tolerate it and we will take decisive countermeasures," the agency quoted the North Korean Foreign Ministry as saying.
"If he sought asylum, it means that he is a renegade and he is dismissed," the ministry said, adding that it had asked Beijing to investigate what it called Hwang's disappearance.

Pyongyang officials had previously been steadfast in their accusation that Seoul abducted the scholarly architect of North Korea's governing ideology of Juche, or self-reliance. South Korea dismissed the charge as preposterous.
Seoul and Beijing were working to find a solution to a crisis that has thrown relations between China and the two Koreas into turmoil, officials said.
"Negotiations with the Chinese government are still going on," said South Korean embassy spokesman Chang Moon Ik, but declined to give details.

South Korean Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung called for extraordinary alertness against the North, Seoul's arch-enemy since the 1950-53 civil war, saying Hwang's defection showed serious instability in the Stalinist hermit kingdom.

But South Korean officials said the softer tone from the North, whose officials had earlier issued dour threats of war and violence if Hwang was compelled to go to Seoul, meant Pyongyang had reconsidered its stance.
"It is certain North Korea is changing its attitude," said Kim Kyung-woong, a senior official at the state South-North Dialogue Office.

North Korean officials, who had kept vigil outside South Korea's Beijing mission since the beginning of the crisis, largely withdrew from the area on Tuesday but the move failed to stop China boosting security in the sedate diplomatic quarter.
China, an unwilling third party in the feuding between the two hostile sides of the Korean peninsula, has appealed to both sides to act calmly to resolve the affair.

The stationing of white armoured personnel carriers along the tree-lined approaches to the South Korean mission bolstered the visible defences that already included scores of regular and paramilitary police armed with assault rifles.
A crowd control truck armed with water cannon and a bullet-proof car have been parked outside the mission for days.
Passing Beijing residents, many of them previously unaware of a diplomatic drama ignored by China's state media, clustered beyond the police cordon for a glimpse of the mission.
"I think this one North Korean guy has made a lot of trouble for China," said one Beijing factory worker who came to watch after hearing about Hwang's defection on shortwave radio.
"This is not a comfortable situation for the Chinese government," he said.
